title: The Kulturforum in Berlin: Gemäldegalerie or Neue Nationalgalerie, and which ticket to buy
subtitle: Two great museums five minutes apart, two smaller ones beside them, and a square most visitors to Berlin never reach.
excerpt: The Kulturforum near Potsdamer Platz holds the old master paintings of the Gemäldegalerie and the modern art of the Neue Nationalgalerie. What each one shows, how long it takes, which to choose, what else is on the square, and what each ticket includes.

how long do you need at the Gemäldegalerie
what is in the Neue Nationalgalerie
what is at the Kulturforum in Berlin
Gemäldegalerie or Museum Island
meta_title: Kulturforum Berlin: Gemäldegalerie or Neue Nationalgalerie
meta_description: Old masters in the Gemäldegalerie or modern art in the Neue Nationalgalerie: what each shows, how long it takes, and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: The black steel roof and glass walls of the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin on its stone terrace, under a blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="gemaldegalerie-berlin" city="berlin"]

When Berlin was divided, its museums were divided too. Museum Island, with the buildings of the old royal collections, lay in the East. Much of what had hung in them had been moved out of the city during the war, ended up in the western zones, and came back to West Berlin, where there was nowhere fitting to show it. For decades the old master paintings hung in a suburban museum in Dahlem.

The answer was a new cultural quarter, planned from the late 1950s on bombed land at the edge of the Tiergarten, a few hundred metres from the line where the Wall went up in 1961. The concert hall of the Berlin Philharmonic opened there in 1963, and a gallery for modern art by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe in 1968. The paintings from Dahlem arrived only in 1998, by which time the Wall was gone. The result is the Kulturforum: a windy square with two of the best museums in Germany on it, and a choice to make if you have half a day.

What is on the square

  • The Gemäldegalerie: European painting from the thirteenth to the eighteenth century. Ticket.
  • The Neue Nationalgalerie: art of the twentieth century, in the building by Mies. Ticket.
  • The Kupferstichkabinett, the museum of prints and drawings, reached through the same entrance hall as the Gemäldegalerie. Ticket.
  • The Kunstgewerbemuseum, the museum of decorative arts. Ticket.
  • The Philharmonie and its smaller chamber music hall, both by Hans Scharoun. You go in for a concert or a guided visit.
  • The Musical Instrument Museum, beside the Philharmonie, with a ticket of its own.
  • St Matthew's Church, built in the 1840s by Friedrich August Stüler: the only building here that is older than the war. Free.

The shared entrance on the square. The names of the museums behind it are on the wall. Photo: Oursana, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The Gemäldegalerie

About a thousand paintings hang in the main gallery, in some seventy rooms laid out as a horseshoe around a long, quiet central hall. Walked from end to end the circuit is close to two kilometres. The northern schools (German, Netherlandish, Dutch) fill one arm, and the Italians, French and Spanish the other.

What people come for:

  • Rembrandt. One of the largest groups of his paintings anywhere, in a room of their own at the far end.
  • Vermeer. Two of the few dozen pictures he painted: The Glass of Wine and Woman with a Pearl Necklace.
  • Bruegel. The Netherlandish Proverbs of 1559, a village in which more than a hundred sayings are acted out at once.
  • Caravaggio. Amor Victorious, a grinning Cupid painted in Rome in about 1602.
  • The Germans. Holbein's portrait of the merchant Georg Gisze, Cranach's Fountain of Youth, and several Dürers.
  • The Italians. Botticelli, Raphael's early Madonnas, Titian.

Allow two to three hours. The rooms are rarely crowded, even in summer, which is the main difference from the museums on the island.

One of the large rooms of the Italian wing of the Gemäldegalerie. Photo: Oursana, via Wikimedia Commons.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Netherlandish Proverbs, 1559, in the Gemäldegalerie. Photo: Google Art Project, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Neue Nationalgalerie

This was the last large building Mies van der Rohe completed. He died in 1969, the year after it opened. It is a flat steel roof about 65 metres square, resting on eight columns, over a hall with walls of glass. The roof was put together on the ground and raised in one piece, in a single day in April 1967.

The glass hall at street level is used for temporary exhibitions. The collection is downstairs, in ordinary rooms that open onto a walled sculpture garden. It covers the twentieth century: Kirchner's Potsdamer Platz of 1914, Beckmann, Dix, Grosz, Klee, and art from both halves of the divided country after 1945. It is shown in changing selections, so a particular picture may not be on the wall when you come.

The building was closed from 2015 to 2021 for a restoration led by David Chipperfield. Allow an hour and a half. It is busier than its neighbour, and a popular exhibition can mean entry by time slot.

Which one

  • You want paintings you already know from books: the Gemäldegalerie.
  • You care about architecture, or about Berlin in the 1920s: the Neue Nationalgalerie.
  • You have a whole afternoon: both. They are five minutes apart on foot. Start with the Gemäldegalerie, which asks for more attention, and finish in the glass hall towards evening.
  • You have already done Museum Island: the Gemäldegalerie is the collection the island lacks. There is very little old master painting on the island itself.

The two smaller museums

The Kupferstichkabinett owns more than half a million prints and over a hundred thousand drawings, among them Botticelli's illustrations to Dante. Paper cannot stay in the light, so there is no permanent display: you see whatever exhibition is on. Look that up first.

The Kunstgewerbemuseum shows craft and design from the Middle Ages to now: the medieval goldsmiths' work of the Guelph Treasure, Renaissance and Baroque pieces, porcelain, a fashion gallery, and twentieth-century design in the basement. An hour is enough.

What each ticket includes

Every museum here sells its own ticket at its own desk. The Berlin state museums have also sold a combined day ticket for the houses of the Kulturforum, and have admitted visitors under 18 free. Most of these museums have been closed on Mondays. In our partner's list:

  • The Gemäldegalerie entrance ticket is entry and nothing else.
  • The Gemäldegalerie ticket with an in-app audio tour adds a route with commentary through the rooms, on your own phone. It is the only listing here with commentary inside a museum. Bring earphones.
  • The Neue Nationalgalerie entry names both the collection and the temporary exhibitions among its inclusions.
  • The Berlin highlights tour with a Neue Nationalgalerie ticket is the same entry with an audio walk that starts outside the gallery and ends at the Red Town Hall. It has no commentary inside.
  • The Kupferstichkabinett and the Museum of Decorative Arts are sold as plain entry tickets. Their listings give few details, so read them before you pay.

[partner city="berlin" match="gemaldegalerie,nationalgalerie,kupferstich,decorative" limit="6"]

Getting there

Potsdamer Platz station is a ten-minute walk away, and city buses stop on the square itself. A new museum for twentieth-century art has been under construction between the Neue Nationalgalerie and the Philharmonie, so expect fences on part of the square, or a new building if it has opened. Current hours are on our pages for the Gemäldegalerie and the Neue Nationalgalerie.

The Philharmonie of 1963, a few steps from the museums. Photo: Tanweer Morshed, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

From here

Potsdamer Platz is ten minutes to the east, with a few slabs of the Wall still standing on the pavement. The Tiergarten begins across the road to the north. Five minutes to the west, the German Resistance Memorial fills the courtyard where the officers of the plot of 20 July 1944 were shot. It is free. See what else there is in Berlin, or open the trip planner for Germany.

Cover photo: Fridolin freudenfett, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like old master painting. It holds Rembrandt, Vermeer, Bruegel, Caravaggio, Holbein and Botticelli in rooms that are rarely crowded.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Gemäldegalerie?
faqs.a: Two to three hours. The circuit through some seventy rooms is close to two kilometres long.

faqs.q: What is in the Neue Nationalgalerie?
faqs.a: Art of the twentieth century, shown in changing selections on the lower floor, and temporary exhibitions in the glass hall above. The building, by Mies van der Rohe, opened in 1968.

faqs.q: Gemäldegalerie or Neue Nationalgalerie: which should you choose?
faqs.a: The Gemäldegalerie for European painting before 1800, the Neue Nationalgalerie for modern art and for its architecture. They are five minutes apart, so an afternoon covers both.

faqs.q: Is the Gemäldegalerie on Museum Island?
faqs.a: No. It is at the Kulturforum, near Potsdamer Platz, about three kilometres from Museum Island, and it has its own ticket.

title: The Albertina in Vienna: Albertina or Albertina Modern, and what the all-locations ticket covers
subtitle: One name on two buildings in the city and on several different tickets: what is behind each of them.
excerpt: What you see at the Albertina (the state rooms, Monet to Picasso, the exhibitions), what the Albertina Modern on Karlsplatz is, which of the two to choose, and what the single, combined and audio tour tickets include.
longtail_phrases: what is the difference between Albertina and Albertina Modern
are the state rooms included in the Albertina ticket
can you see Dürer's hare at the Albertina
how long do you need at the Albertina
is the Albertina open on Mondays
meta_title: Albertina or Albertina Modern in Vienna: which ticket
meta_description: The Albertina, the Albertina Modern and the combined ticket: what each covers, whether the state rooms are included, and which one to choose.

featured_image.alt: The Albertina in Vienna on its raised bastion, with a long metal roof projecting over the entrance and an equestrian statue on the terrace

content_html:
[place attraction="albertina" city="vienna"]

Albert of Saxe-Teschen was a younger son of the Elector of Saxony, with a title and not much money. In 1766 he married Marie Christine, the favourite daughter of Empress Maria Theresa, who was allowed to choose her own husband and came with a very large dowry. He spent a good part of it on paper. From 1776 he collected drawings and prints with a plan, school by school, and he went on for nearly fifty years, through a governorship in Brussels that the French Revolution brought to an end.

He settled in Vienna, in a palace on a surviving stretch of the city wall, and died there in 1822. What he left is one of the largest collections of drawings and prints in the world: about 65,000 drawings and around a million prints, Dürer's Young Hare among them. The palace took his name. Today that name is on two buildings in the city and on several kinds of ticket, and it is worth knowing what is behind each before you pay.

Three things in one building

The Albertina stands on its bastion behind the State Opera. One ticket covers everything in it, and there are three parts.

  • The state rooms. About twenty rooms on the main floor, furnished in the 1820s for Archduke Charles, Albert's adopted heir and the general who beat Napoleon at Aspern in 1809. Silk on the walls, inlaid floors, and the Hall of the Muses, with statues of Apollo and the nine muses. Good copies of the most famous drawings hang here.
  • Monet to Picasso. A permanent hanging of modern painting, the Batliner Collection, on loan to the museum since 2007: the French Impressionists, Cézanne, the German Expressionists, the Russian avant-garde, Picasso.
  • The exhibitions. Usually two or three at once. This is where original drawings from the collection come out, for a few months at a time.

Allow two hours for the building: half an hour for the state rooms and the rest divided as you like.

One of the state rooms, hung with yellow silk. Photo: Thomas Ledl, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The room shown as the study of Archduke Charles. Photo: Thomas Ledl, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

About the hare

Dürer painted the Young Hare in watercolour in 1502. Works on paper fade in light, so the original spends most of its life in a dark store and is shown for a short period every few years. What you see the rest of the time, in the state rooms, is a facsimile. The same goes for his Praying Hands. If the hare is your reason for coming, check whether an exhibition with the original is running. If it is not, the visit is still worth making, for the rooms and the paintings.

Albrecht Dürer, Young Hare, 1502. The original is shown only rarely. Photo: Google Art Project, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Albertina Modern

The second house opened in 2020 in the Künstlerhaus on Karlsplatz, an exhibition hall that the artists' society of Vienna built for itself in the 1860s, beside the Musikverein. It shows art made after 1945, Austrian and international, and it has no permanent hanging: the whole building is given to changing exhibitions. What you see depends entirely on the month.

It is ten minutes on foot from the Albertina, past the Opera and across the Ring. A visit takes about an hour.

A third house, in Klosterneuburg outside the city, opened in 2024 for large contemporary works. It has been open only for part of the year.

The Künstlerhaus on Karlsplatz, home of the Albertina Modern since 2020. Photo: C.Stadler/Bwag, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which one

  • First visit to Vienna, one museum: the Albertina. It gives you a Habsburg interior and a short history of modern painting in the same two hours.
  • You follow contemporary art: look at what the Albertina Modern is showing, and go if the exhibition interests you.
  • Both: possible in one afternoon, since they are so close. Do the Albertina first.
  • Old masters on canvas: neither. Those are in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

What the tickets cover

Each house sells its own ticket, and there is a combined one. In our partner's list:

  • The Albertina Palace ticket with an audio tour includes entry to the Albertina. The commentary, in the partner's app on your own phone, covers the state rooms only. The listing says plainly that it does not cover the art collection or the temporary exhibitions.
  • The Albertina Palace audio tour without the word ticket in its name is that same commentary alone. Entry is listed among the things not included, so you buy it separately.
  • The Albertina Modern ticket with a city walk audio tour is entry to the house on Karlsplatz and an audio walk through the streets. There is no commentary inside.
  • The all-locations ticket is described as one ticket for both houses in Vienna. The listing does not spell out its inclusions. Before you pay, read on it whether Klosterneuburg counts as a location and for how long the second visit stays valid.

These are the Albertina tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="vienna" match="albertina" limit="4"]

Practical

The entrance is up on the bastion. An escalator and a staircase climb from Albertinaplatz to the terrace, under the long metal roof that the architect Hans Hollein added in 2003. The terrace is free and looks down on the Opera and the Burggarten.

Unlike many museums in Vienna, the Albertina has been open every day, Mondays included, with late opening on some evenings. Go to the state rooms first: they are small, and they fill when the groups arrive. Hours are on our pages for the Albertina and the Albertina Modern.

From here

Behind the Albertina is the Burggarten, with the Mozart monument and the glass Palm House. The Hofburg begins next door, and the Imperial Crypt, where the Habsburgs are buried, is three minutes away. On Albertinaplatz itself stands the Memorial against War and Fascism by Alfred Hrdlicka, from 1988. See what else there is in Vienna, or open the trip planner for Austria.

Cover photo: C.Stadler/Bwag, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Albertina and the Albertina Modern?
faqs.a: The Albertina is the palace behind the Opera, with state rooms, a permanent hanging from Monet to Picasso and exhibitions. The Albertina Modern, on Karlsplatz, shows changing exhibitions of art made after 1945.

faqs.q: Are the state rooms included in the Albertina ticket?
faqs.a: Yes. One ticket to the Albertina covers the state rooms, the permanent hanging and the temporary exhibitions in the building.

faqs.q: Can you see Dürer's Young Hare at the Albertina?
faqs.a: Usually only as a facsimile. The original watercolour of 1502 is sensitive to light and is shown for a short period every few years.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Albertina?
faqs.a: About two hours: half an hour for the state rooms and the rest for the paintings and one exhibition. The Albertina Modern takes about an hour.

faqs.q: Does the all-locations ticket cover both Albertina museums?
faqs.a: It is described as one ticket for the Albertina and the Albertina Modern. Check on the listing whether the third house in Klosterneuburg is included and how long the ticket stays valid.

title: Prague on a rainy day: which museum to choose, and what each ticket includes
subtitle: Five indoor choices in a city whose main sights are all outdoors, and what the bundled tickets really contain.
excerpt: The Museum of Communism, the Franz Kafka Museum, the Lobkowicz Palace, the National Technical Museum and the Museum Story of Prague: what each is, who it suits, how long it takes, and what the partner bundles with the ticket.
secondary_keywords: what to do in Prague when it rains
longtail_phrases: what to do in Prague on a rainy day
is the Museum of Communism in Prague worth it
is the Kafka Museum in Prague worth visiting

meta_title: Prague on a rainy day: which museum, which ticket
meta_description: Five museums for a wet day in Prague: what each one is, who it suits, how long it takes, and what the tickets sold with an audio walk really include.

featured_image.alt: Wet cobbles of Charles Bridge in Prague at night, with the lit towers of the Lesser Town and the castle beyond

content_html:
[place attraction="museum-of-communism-prague" city="prague"]

In 2001, twelve years after communist rule ended in Czechoslovakia, a museum about it opened in Prague. The state had nothing to do with it. Its founder was Glenn Spicker, an American who had come to the city after 1989 and opened a bar and a bagel shop, and who went round junk shops and flea markets buying the busts, posters and uniforms that nobody wanted any more. He rented rooms in a palace on the smartest shopping street, above a McDonald's and beside a casino, and the museum's posters made the most of the address.

In 2017 the museum moved to larger rooms near Republic Square, and it is still one of the first places named in Prague when the sky turns grey. That happens more than visitors expect. The city's main sights are a bridge, a castle hill and a set of squares, all out of doors, and the wettest months here are the summer ones, when most people come. So here are five indoor choices, and what the tickets sold for them really contain.

The Museum of Communism

The rooms run in order of time, from the takeover of February 1948 to the demonstrations of November 1989. Between the panels there are reconstructions: a shop with almost nothing on the shelves, a schoolroom, a workshop, an interrogation room. The 1968 invasion and the film of the crowds in 1989 are the parts people remember.

There is a great deal to read, all of it in English as well as Czech. Allow an hour and a half to two hours. It suits adults and older teenagers, and small children will be bored. It has been open every day, which helps on a Monday, when much else in Prague is shut.

A reconstructed workshop in the Museum of Communism. Photo: Ferfive, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The Franz Kafka Museum

Kafka was born in Prague in 1883, a few steps from the Old Town Square. He wrote in German, worked for an insurance institute, published little, and died in 1924. The exhibition about him was made for Barcelona in 1999 and has been in Prague since 2005, in a former brickworks on the river bank of the Lesser Town, close to Charles Bridge.

It shows first editions, letters, diaries and drawings, in dark rooms with sound and film. It is about a mood as much as about documents, and it works best if you have read him. An hour is enough. In the courtyard, free to see, is a fountain by the sculptor David Černý that makes most visitors laugh.

The door of the Kafka Museum, marked by two letters K. Photo: Perituss, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The Lobkowicz Palace

This palace stands inside the castle precinct, at its lower, eastern end, and it is the one building there in private hands. It was taken from the Lobkowicz family twice, by the Nazis and then by the communists, returned in 2002 and opened in 2007. The castle's own ticket does not cover it.

The collection is a family's, and a remarkable one: Bruegel's Haymaking of 1565, two views of the Thames by Canaletto, and scores by Beethoven, whose patron was a Prince Lobkowicz. The visit has usually come with an audio guide in which the family tells the story. Allow an hour and a half. The drawback in rain is the approach: an uphill walk and an outdoor security line at the castle gates.

The Lobkowicz Palace, at the lower end of the castle precinct. Photo: Erudy, via Wikimedia Commons.

The National Technical Museum

On the Letná plateau, north of the river, in a building of the late 1930s. The museum was founded in 1908 and reopened in 2011 after a long renovation. Its transport hall is the reason to come: aircraft hang from the roof above steam locomotives, Czech cars of every decade and rows of motorcycles, with three galleries around them.

Other floors cover astronomy, photography, printing and household technology. With children this is the best wet-day choice in the city, and two to three hours go quickly. Take a tram up, and check the closing day: it has been Monday.

The transport hall of the National Technical Museum. Photo: High Contrast, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0 DE.

The Museum Story of Prague

A recent exhibition on the small square at the Old Town end of Charles Bridge. As the partner's listing describes it, three floors go through the city's past: the Middle Ages and the Hussite wars, then the Nazi and Soviet occupations, then 1989 and after. It is a quick overview in a very central place. We found little independent detail about it, so read recent reviews on the listing before you choose it over the others.

Which one for whom

  • You want to understand the country you are in: the Museum of Communism.
  • You are travelling with children: the National Technical Museum.
  • You like paintings and music: the Lobkowicz Palace, on a day when you are going up to the castle anyway.
  • You have read Kafka: his museum. If you have not, choose something else.
  • You have one hour between showers: the Kafka Museum or the Story of Prague, both beside the bridge.

What the partner's tickets bundle

  • The Museum of Communism ticket is sold together with an audio walk through the city, in the partner's app. The listing says there is no commentary inside the museum. The walk is outdoors, so keep it for a dry hour.
  • The Kafka Museum ticket with a city walk works the same way. Its listed starting point is by St Vitus Cathedral, up at the castle, while the museum stands down by the river: read the meeting point note before you set out.
  • The Museum Story of Prague is a plain entry ticket.
  • The Lobkowicz Palace and the National Technical Museum each have a listing with an audio walk too, but both were marked unavailable when we looked. If they do not appear below, buy at the door.
  • The list also holds a chocolate museum with a workshop, a wax museum and a Banksy show. They are indoors as well, and a different kind of afternoon.

These are the indoor tickets our partner sells in Prague, with today's prices:

[partner city="prague" match="communism,kafka,story,lobkowicz,technical" limit="6"]

Staying dry in between

The metro connects Republic Square with the Lesser Town in a few minutes, and trams climb to the castle and to Letná. Around Wenceslas Square a network of covered shopping passages lets you cross whole blocks under a roof. The best known is the Lucerna passage, where another Černý sculpture, a king riding an upside-down horse, hangs from the ceiling. Hours for the museums are on our pages for the Museum of Communism, the Franz Kafka Museum and the National Technical Museum.

From here

When the rain stops, the Kafka Museum leaves you two minutes from Charles Bridge, and the Museum of Communism five minutes from the Powder Tower and the Old Town. From the Technical Museum, Letná Park is across the road, with a wide view of the river and its bridges. See what else there is in Prague, or open the trip planner for Czechia.

Cover photo: Ulrich Peters, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: What can you do in Prague on a rainy day?
faqs.a: Choose a museum: the Museum of Communism for recent history, the National Technical Museum with children, the Lobkowicz Palace for paintings and music, the Franz Kafka Museum for his readers. The covered passages around Wenceslas Square keep you dry in between.

faqs.q: Is the Museum of Communism in Prague worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, for adults and older teenagers. It tells the story from 1948 to 1989 with reconstructed rooms and a lot of text in English, and takes an hour and a half to two hours.

faqs.q: Is the Kafka Museum in Prague worth visiting?
faqs.a: If you have read Kafka, yes. It is a dark, atmospheric exhibition of first editions, letters and drawings that takes about an hour. If you have not read him, another museum will give you more.

faqs.q: Is the Lobkowicz Palace included in the Prague Castle ticket?
faqs.a: No. It stands inside the castle precinct but is privately owned, and it has its own ticket.

faqs.q: Which museum in Prague is best for children?
faqs.a: The National Technical Museum on Letná. Its transport hall has aircraft hanging above locomotives, cars and motorcycles, and a visit fills two to three hours.

title: Edinburgh indoors and underground: Mary King's Close, the Dungeon, and the museums that are free
subtitle: A buried street, a horror show that is often mistaken for it, and two national museums that cost nothing to enter.
excerpt: What The Real Mary King's Close and the Edinburgh Dungeon each are and which to book, what the free National Museum of Scotland and Scottish National Gallery offer, and what the audio tours sold for them include.
focus_keyword: Mary King's Close or Edinburgh Dungeon
secondary_keywords: National Museum of Scotland audio tour
longtail_phrases: is Mary King's Close worth it
what is the difference between Mary King's Close and the Edinburgh Dungeon
is the National Museum of Scotland free
what to do in Edinburgh when it rains
where is the Great Tapestry of Scotland
meta_title: Edinburgh indoors: Mary King's Close, Dungeon, free museums
meta_description: Mary King's Close or the Edinburgh Dungeon, and the two national museums that are free: what each is, how long it takes, and what the tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The Grand Gallery of the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh: a long hall under a glass roof with tiers of white cast-iron balconies

content_html:
[place attraction="national-museum-of-scotland" city="edinburgh"]

The Old Town of Edinburgh stands on a ridge, and for centuries the only way to fit more people onto it was to build upwards and down the slopes. Narrow lanes called closes ran off the High Street like the bones of a fish, between houses of seven storeys and more. In 1753 the town council decided to build a Royal Exchange for its merchants on the north side of the street. The builders did not clear the slope. They took the tops off the houses in the way and used the lower floors as foundations.

One of the lanes buried like this was Mary King's Close, named after a merchant who lived in it in the 1630s. Its lower end stayed inhabited until 1902. The Exchange became the City Chambers, where the council still meets, and the street underneath is now the best-known ticket in Edinburgh. It is also one of two "underground" attractions that visitors confuse, in a city whose best indoor hours cost nothing at all.

The Real Mary King's Close

This is the real thing: rooms and a steep street of the seventeenth century, under a working council building. You see it on a guided tour of about an hour, in a small group, led by a guide who plays a past resident. The stories are of ordinary lives, and of the plague of 1645. The old tale that the sick were walled in and left to die is a legend, and the tour says so.

What to know before you book:

  • Entry is at a fixed time. In summer, and above all during the August festivals, the day sells out.
  • There are many steps, uneven and sloping floors, low ceilings and dim light. There is no lift.
  • There is a minimum age for children. Check it if yours are small.
  • Photography has not been allowed on the tour.
  • The door is on the High Street, opposite St Giles' Cathedral, in Warriston's Close.

The way in to The Real Mary King's Close, off the High Street. Photo: Mario RM, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

The City Chambers, begun in 1753 as the Royal Exchange. The close lies beneath it. Photo: Jza84, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The Edinburgh Dungeon

The Dungeon, on Market Street beside Waverley station, is not a historic place. It is a show: actors, sets, special effects and a couple of rides, in a visit of a little over an hour that moves from room to room. The material is the dark side of Scottish history, played for frights and laughs: the witch trials, the cannibal Sawney Bean, and Burke and Hare, who in 1828 murdered at least sixteen people to sell the bodies to an anatomy lecturer.

It is loud and dark, with sudden noises, and the operator's guidance is that it does not suit younger children. Entry is by time slot.

And the vaults

A third thing shares the word underground: the vaults in the arches of the South Bridge, finished in 1788. They are shown by separate tour companies. Our partner does not sell them.

Which one to book

  • You want history, told on the spot where it happened: Mary King's Close.
  • You have teenagers who want to be scared: the Dungeon.
  • Both in one day: more than most people enjoy. Choose one, and spend the rest of the wet day in a museum.

The museums that are free

The National Museum of Scotland

On Chambers Street, five minutes south of the High Street. Entry is free. It is two buildings joined together. The Victorian one opened in 1866 around the Grand Gallery, a hall of cast iron and glass. The sandstone wing beside it, added in 1998, tells the story of Scotland.

Look for Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, born near Edinburgh in 1996; eleven of the Lewis chessmen, carved from walrus ivory in the twelfth century; and the Maiden, the beheading machine the city used from the 1560s. A roof terrace looks across to the castle. The museum can fill a day, so choose two floors.

Dolly the sheep, in the National Museum of Scotland. Photo: Sgerbic, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Scottish National Gallery

On the Mound, between the Old Town and the New, in a temple-fronted building by William Playfair that opened in 1859. Entry is free. It is small enough for an hour and a half: Raeburn's skating minister, an early Velázquez of an old woman cooking eggs, Titian, Rembrandt, and a set of rooms for Scottish art opened in 2023.

A room of the Scottish National Gallery on the Mound. Photo: LordHarris, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the partner sells for them

Audio tours only. Both listings say clearly that entry is free and that you are paying for a route with commentary in the partner's app, on your own phone, with your own earphones. The museum tour is listed at three to four hours and the gallery tour at two. Special exhibitions are not included.

A tapestry that is not in Edinburgh

The partner's Edinburgh list includes the Great Tapestry of Scotland, with an address on High Street. That High Street is in Galashiels, in the Borders, about an hour by train from Waverley. The tapestry is 160 embroidered panels on the history of Scotland, stitched by around a thousand volunteers and finished in 2013, and it has had its own building since 2021. It makes a good half-day trip. It is not a way to fill an hour of rain on the Royal Mile.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Real Mary King's Close entry ticket is a place on the guided tour. The listing gives no list of inclusions, so read how the time is chosen.
  • The Edinburgh Dungeon entry ticket is the show alone.
  • The sightseeing tour with a Dungeon ticket adds an audio walk through the city, outdoors. There is no commentary inside.
  • The two museum audio tours and the tapestry ticket, as described above.

These are the indoor tickets and audio tours our partner sells in Edinburgh, with today's prices:

[partner city="edinburgh" match="dungeon,tapestry,close,national" limit="6"]

A wet day in order

Everything here except the tapestry lies within ten minutes' walk. Start at the National Museum when it opens. Book the Close for the early afternoon and eat near the High Street. Finish in the gallery on the Mound, which is on the way to the New Town and the station. Opening hours are on our pages for the National Museum of Scotland and the Scottish National Gallery.

From here

St Giles' Cathedral, across the street from the Close, is open to visitors without a ticket. Below the gallery, Princes Street Gardens fill the valley where a loch once lay, and the New Town begins on the far side. See what else there is in Edinburgh, or open the trip planner for the United Kingdom.

Cover photo: Elshad, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is Mary King's Close worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want real history. It is a guided tour of about an hour through seventeenth-century rooms and a street buried under the City Chambers. Book ahead, and expect steps and uneven floors.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Mary King's Close and the Edinburgh Dungeon?
faqs.a: Mary King's Close is a real buried street shown on a guided tour. The Edinburgh Dungeon is a show with actors, sets and rides about the dark side of Scottish history.

faqs.q: Is the National Museum of Scotland free?
faqs.a: Yes, entry is free. The audio tour our partner sells for it is commentary only, and its listing says so.

faqs.q: What can you do in Edinburgh when it rains?
faqs.a: Visit the National Museum of Scotland and the Scottish National Gallery, both free, and book a tour of The Real Mary King's Close. All three are within ten minutes' walk of each other.

faqs.q: Where is the Great Tapestry of Scotland?
faqs.a: In Galashiels, in the Scottish Borders, about an hour by train from Edinburgh Waverley. It is not in Edinburgh itself.

title: Montjuïc in Barcelona: which of the two cable cars, the castle, and what is free on the hill
subtitle: Three machines go up the hill and two of them are called cable cars. Which is which, and what to pay for at the top.
excerpt: How to get up Montjuïc (the cable car, the port cable car, the funicular), what the castle offers, what is free on the hill, how the Miró Foundation, the MNAC and the Poble Espanyol compare, and what the partner tickets include.
focus_keyword: Montjuïc cable car or port cable car
longtail_phrases: which cable car goes to Montjuïc castle
is the Montjuïc cable car worth it
how to get to Montjuïc castle without the cable car
what is free to see on Montjuïc
is Poble Espanyol worth visiting
meta_title: Montjuïc Barcelona: which cable car, castle, what is free
meta_description: The Montjuïc cable car, the port cable car and the funicular: which goes where, what the castle offers, what is free on the hill, what tickets include.

featured_image.alt: Gondolas of the Montjuïc cable car above the trees, with the roofs of Barcelona spread out behind them

content_html:
[place attraction="montjuic-castle" city="barcelona"]

Most castles were built to defend a city. The one on Montjuïc spent much of its life pointed at the city below it. The fortress took its present star shape in the second half of the eighteenth century, after Barcelona had fallen to the Bourbon army in 1714, and its guns covered the streets as well as the sea. In 1842 General Espartero had the city shelled from it to end a revolt. Later it was a military prison. On 15 October 1940 Lluís Companys, the elected president of Catalonia, arrested in exile in France and handed over to Franco's government, was shot in its moat.

The army gave the castle up to the city only in 2007. The hill around it had by then been remade twice, for the International Exposition of 1929 and for the Olympic Games of 1992. Today Montjuïc holds a fortress, several museums, a dozen gardens and three different machines for getting up, two of which are called cable cars. Sorting those out is the first job.

Two cable cars and a funicular

  • The Montjuïc cable car (Telefèric de Montjuïc). Small modern gondolas for eight people. They leave from Avinguda Miramar, halfway up the hill, and climb about 750 metres to the gate of the castle, with a stop at a viewpoint on the way. It has its own ticket, and ordinary city transport tickets are not valid on it. This is the one our partner sells.
  • The port cable car (Telefèric del Port). Old red cabins, in which you stand, that cross the harbour high above the water from a steel tower at Barceloneta to Miramar, on the seaward slope of Montjuïc. It was planned for the 1929 exposition and opened in 1931. It is run by a different company, with a different ticket and long lines in summer. It does not go to the castle: from where it lands, the other cable car is a ten-minute walk and the castle is far above.
  • The funicular. It runs from Paral·lel metro station up to Avinguda Miramar, mostly in a tunnel, and arrives beside the lower station of the Montjuïc cable car. It belongs to the metro network, so an ordinary transport ticket covers it. It closes for maintenance from time to time, and a bus replaces it.

A city bus also climbs from Plaça d'Espanya to the castle gate. So the cable car is never necessary. You take it for the view over the whole city.

The port cable car: the red cabin that crosses the harbour. It does not go to the castle. Photo: CGE, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The castle

Entry is paid, and the castle has had free hours on Sunday afternoons, so check before you go. Inside are the parade ground, a walk around the ramparts and bastions, a watchtower, and rooms on the history of the hill. The walls look over the port on one side and the city on the other. An hour is enough.

Without a ticket you can still walk round the outside of the walls, look into the moat with its gardens, and stand at the viewpoint beside the gate.

The parade ground of the castle, with its watchtower. Photo: Txllxt TxllxT, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free on the hill

  • The gardens. The cactus garden of Mossèn Costa i Llobera, on the slope above the port. The Laribal gardens, with tiled stairs and running water. The Joan Brossa gardens, on the site of an old amusement park.
  • The viewpoints. The Mirador de l'Alcalde below the castle, Miramar, and the terrace in front of the Palau Nacional, which looks down the avenue to Plaça d'Espanya.
  • The Olympic ring. The stadium of 1929, rebuilt inside for 1992, the Palau Sant Jordi arena by Arata Isozaki, and the white communications tower by Santiago Calatrava.
  • The Magic Fountain, at the foot of the hill, built for 1929. Its evening shows cost nothing when they run. They have been stopped in years of drought, so check.

The museums and the Poble Espanyol

The Fundació Joan Miró

Opened in 1975 in a white building by Josep Lluís Sert, a friend of the painter, and lit by daylight. Paintings, sculpture and textiles from Miró's whole life, and a fountain of mercury by Alexander Calder. Allow an hour and a half. It is a short walk from the top of the funicular.

The MNAC

The national art museum of Catalonia fills the Palau Nacional, the domed palace of 1929. Its Romanesque section is like nothing else: wall paintings taken about a century ago from small churches in the Pyrenees and remounted on rebuilt apses, among them the Christ in Majesty from Sant Climent de Taüll, painted in 1123. Allow two hours.

The Palau Nacional of 1929, home of the national art museum of Catalonia. Photo: Felix König, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The Poble Espanyol

A village of more than a hundred buildings copied at full size from every region of Spain, put up for the 1929 exposition and meant to be pulled down afterwards. Today it has craft workshops, restaurants and a small museum of modern art. It is the easiest choice with children.

A square in the Poble Espanyol, built for the exposition of 1929. Photo: Enric, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Mies van der Rohe Pavilion

The German pavilion of 1929, by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich: marble, glass, steel and two pools. It was taken down in 1930 and rebuilt on the same spot in the 1980s. Twenty minutes.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The cable car ticket is a round trip on the Montjuïc cable car. The listing says that entry to the castle is not included.
  • The "Montjuic Entry and Cable Car" audio tour is the same round trip with an audio tour of the hill in the partner's app. Despite the word entry, its listing excludes tickets to the museums and sights on the way.
  • The Fundació Joan Miró listing promises a skip-the-line ticket in its title, but its list of inclusions names only an audio tour of the park. Check what is listed before you pay.
  • The MNAC and Poble Espanyol tickets each come with an audio walk through other parts of Barcelona, not the hill. There is no commentary inside.
  • The pavilion is a plain entry ticket.

These are the Montjuïc tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="barcelona" match="montjuic,mies,nacional,poble" limit="6"]

A downhill route

Take the funicular up, then the cable car to the castle. Walk down through the gardens to the Miró Foundation, on past the Olympic stadium to the terrace of the Palau Nacional, and down the outdoor escalators to the fountain. The pavilion and the Poble Espanyol are five minutes to the west. You finish at the metro of Plaça d'Espanya, between three and four kilometres from the castle, almost all of it downhill. There is little shade near the top, so carry water in summer. Hours are on our pages for Montjuïc Castle and the Montjuïc cable car.

From here

Plaça d'Espanya has metro lines to the whole city. See our pages for the Fundació Joan Miró, the MNAC and the rest of Barcelona, or open the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Which cable car goes to Montjuïc Castle?
faqs.a: The Montjuïc cable car, with small gondolas, from Avinguda Miramar to the castle gate. The red port cable car crosses the harbour from Barceloneta and stops at Miramar, far below the castle.

faqs.q: Is the Montjuïc cable car worth it?
faqs.a: For the view over the city, yes. It is not needed to reach the castle: a city bus goes to the gate, and the funicular covers the first half of the climb on an ordinary transport ticket.

faqs.q: How do you get to Montjuïc Castle without the cable car?
faqs.a: By city bus from Plaça d'Espanya to the castle gate, or by funicular from Paral·lel metro station and then an uphill walk through the gardens.

faqs.q: What is free to see on Montjuïc?
faqs.a: The gardens, the viewpoints, the outside of the castle walls, the Olympic ring from outside, the terrace of the Palau Nacional and, when they run, the shows of the Magic Fountain.

faqs.q: Is the Poble Espanyol worth visiting?
faqs.a: With children, or if you will not see the rest of Spain, yes. It is a village of full-size copies of buildings from every Spanish region, built in 1929, with craft workshops and restaurants.
